title: Ice floats because water does something almost nothing else does
body: Most substances shrink when they freeze, so their solid sinks in their own liquid. Water does the opposite. As it freezes, hydrogen bonds lock its V-shaped molecules into an open, hexagonal lattice with lots of empty space, making ice about 9% less dense than liquid water. That one quirk shapes our planet: ice forms a floating lid on lakes and oceans, insulating the water below and letting life survive the winter.

slides.question: How much less dense is ice than liquid water?
slides.explanation: About 9%. As water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock its molecules into an open hexagonal lattice full of empty space, so ice floats as a lid on lakes and oceans.

slides.heading: Densest at 4 °C
slides.text: Liquid water is densest at about 4 °C. In winter that water sinks to the bottom of lakes while colder water rises, so lakes freeze from the top down.

slides.heading: Pipes and potholes
slides.text: Freezing water expands with enough force to burst pipes and split rocks. Repeated freeze–thaw cycles crack roads and help wear down mountains.

slides.heading: A tiny club
slides.text: Only a handful of substances also expand when they solidify, including silicon, gallium and bismuth.
